title: Why a Win Is Never Due
question: Can any clever betting plan beat a fair game?
hook: Doubling your bet after every loss sounds like a sure way to win, so why does it bankrupt people?
idea: In a fair game the expected next value equals the present one, so past results never make a win due.

beats.prompt: A gambler flips a fair coin and doubles the bet after every loss, with a limited bankroll. What eventually happens?

choices.label: The gambler is certain to finish with a profit
choices.feedback: It seems a sure thing since heads will come eventually, but the bets grow so fast that a finite bankroll runs out first.

choices.label: The gambler's wealth just hovers around the start
choices.feedback: This misses how fast bets grow: doubling after each loss makes them explode.

choices.label: The growing bets eventually bankrupt the gambler

beats.explain: Doubling lets the first win recover all losses, but the exponential growth of bets eventually bankrupts users with finite bankrolls.

beats.prompt: Put the doubling strategy in the order it plays out.
items: The gambler bets a stake on a coin flip
The coin comes up tails and the stake is lost
A win recovers all earlier losses plus the original stake
beats.explain: The gambler doubles after every loss so that the first win recovers all previous losses and wins a profit equal to the original stake.

beats.prompt: Match each person to their role in martingale theory.
pairs: Did much of the original theory development
beats.explain: Lévy introduced the idea without naming it, Ville named it later, and Doob among others developed much of the early theory.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which one?
steps: A fair coin gives a win or a loss of my stake with equal chances.
I have lost five tosses in a row.
So a win is due, and my expected fortune after the next toss is higher.
I should bet more on the next toss.
beats.explain: For a fair game the expected fortune after the next game equals the present fortune, regardless of past outcomes.
